title: Stage 6: Dependency injection
summary: Move storage behind an ITaskStore interface and let ASP.NET Core inject it into your endpoints.

steps.title: Program.cs is doing two jobs
body: Look at your `Program.cs`. It does two unrelated jobs:
1. **HTTP**: routes, binding, validation, status codes.
2. **Storage**: the list, finding a task by id, choosing the next id, replacing, removing.
The storage code is spread through the endpoint lambdas, and every one of them reaches for the same `tasks` variable. That holds you back in three ways:
- Moving from a list to a database would mean rewriting every endpoint.
- The storage rules cannot be tested without starting a web server.
- A change to storage risks breaking the HTTP behaviour, and the reverse.
The cure is one you have used before: put the storage behind an **interface** and hand the endpoints something that implements it.
```csharp
interface INoteStore
IReadOnlyList<Note> GetAll();
Note Add(string text);
class InMemoryNoteStore : INoteStore
private readonly List<Note> _notes = new();
public IReadOnlyList<Note> GetAll() => _notes.ToList();
public Note Add(string text)
var note = new Note(_notes.Count + 1, text);
_notes.Add(note);
return note;
The endpoints will know only `INoteStore`. Whether a list or a database sits behind it becomes a detail they cannot see.
In the lesson track you wired dependencies together by hand. ASP.NET Core has a **dependency injection container** that does the wiring, and this stage uses it.

steps.prompt: The endpoints depend on `ITaskStore` instead of on a `List<TaskItem>`. What does that buy you?
options: A database-backed store can replace the in-memory one without changing any endpoint.
Requests are answered faster, because interface calls skip the list.
The tasks now survive a restart of the server.
The JSON no longer needs camelCase property names.
steps.explain: The interface is a seam: everything on the HTTP side talks to `ITaskStore`, so a different implementation slots in behind it. Nothing gets faster and nothing is persisted. The data still lives in memory until someone writes a store that saves it.

steps.title: Registering and injecting a service
body: Dependency injection in ASP.NET Core has two halves.
**Register**: before the app is built, tell the container which class to use when someone asks for the interface.
```csharp
var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);
builder.Services.AddSingleton<INoteStore, InMemoryNoteStore>();
var app = builder.Build();
Read it as: *when anything needs an `INoteStore`, give it the `InMemoryNoteStore`.* Registration goes before `builder.Build()`, because building is what freezes the list of services.
**Inject**: ask for the interface as a handler parameter.
```csharp
app.MapGet("/notes", (INoteStore store) => store.GetAll());
app.MapPost("/notes", (CreateNote request, INoteStore store) =>
Results.Created("/notes", store.Add(request.Text ?? "")));
You never write `new InMemoryNoteStore()`. The container creates it and passes it in.
## How does a parameter get its value?
A handler can now have parameters from four places. The framework decides per parameter:
| Parameter | Comes from | Because |
| `int id` | the route | the route has `{id}` |
| `bool? done` | the query string | simple type, not in the route |
| `ITaskStore store` | the container | its type is a registered service |
| `CreateTask request` | the JSON body | a complex type that is not a service |

> **Tip:** If you forget to register the service, the framework assumes `ITaskStore store` must be the body, and the app fails at startup because a GET cannot have one. An odd error about a body on a GET usually means a missing registration.

steps.title: Lifetimes: singleton, scoped, transient
body: When you register a service you also choose its **lifetime**: how long one instance lives, and so who shares it.
| Registration | One instance per | Typical use |
| `AddSingleton` | the whole application | shared state, caches, anything expensive to build |
| `AddScoped` | HTTP request | a database session for the work of one request |
| `AddTransient` | time it is asked for | small helpers with no state |
For an in-memory store the choice decides whether the API works at all. The store *is* the data:
- **Singleton**: one store for the life of the server. A task created by one request is there for the next. Correct.
- **Scoped**: every request gets a brand-new store, seeded with the three starting tasks. A `POST` adds a task, the request ends, and the store is thrown away. The next `GET` never sees it.
- **Transient**: the same loss, even sooner.
So an in-memory store must be a singleton. A store backed by a database is usually scoped instead: the data lives in the database, and each request gets its own short-lived connection to it.

steps.prompt: Two factories stand in for two lifetimes: one always hands out the same object, the other makes a new one each time. What does this print?
steps.explain: Every call to `singleton()` returns the same counter, so both `Add` calls land on it. Every call to `transient()` builds a fresh counter: the two that were incremented are already gone, and the one being printed has never been touched. That is what happens to your tasks if the store is not a singleton.

items: An in-memory store that must remember tasks between requests
A database session that should cover exactly one request
A cache of exchange rates shared by all users
A tiny stateless helper that formats dates
An object that collects the changes made during the current request
steps.explain: Ask who has to share the instance. Everyone, forever: singleton. Everything inside one request: scoped. Nobody: transient.

steps.title: One store, many requests
body: A web server handles many requests **at the same time**, on different threads. A singleton is one object, so all of those threads call into the same store at once.
`List<T>` is not built for that. Picture two `POST` requests arriving together:
1. Request A reads the highest id: 3.
2. Request B reads the highest id: 3.
3. A adds task 4.
4. B adds task 4 as well. Two tasks now share an id.
Two threads changing a list at the same moment can even corrupt it.
The fix is to let only one thread at a time into the code that touches the list. C# has a statement for it:
```csharp
private readonly object _gate = new();
public Note Add(string text)
lock (_gate)
var note = new Note(_notes.Count + 1, text);
_notes.Add(note);
return note;
A thread that reaches `lock (_gate)` while another thread is inside waits until that one leaves. Reading the id and adding the task now happen as one uninterrupted step.

Guard every method that touches the list, reads included. And when you hand the tasks out, return a **copy** (`_tasks.ToList()`): a caller looping over the real list while another request changes it would crash.
This is a real advantage of the store class. The locking lives in one place, and no endpoint has to remember it.

steps.prompt: Why does `GetAll()` return `_tasks.ToList()` from inside the lock, and not `_tasks` itself?
options: The caller gets a snapshot that no other request can change while it is being read.
A `List<TaskItem>` cannot be returned as an `IReadOnlyList<TaskItem>`.
Copying the list is faster than returning it.
steps.explain: The lock protects the list only while the method runs. Once `GetAll` returns, the caller is outside the lock, so it must hold its own copy. Handing out the real list would let a request loop over it while another request adds to it.

steps.title: Write the store
prompt: Move the storage code into its own types. In this step you write and register them. The endpoints stay as they are until the next step.
At the bottom of the file, add an interface with exactly these members:
```csharp
interface ITaskStore
IReadOnlyList<TaskItem> GetAll();
TaskItem? Get(int id);
TaskItem Add(string title);
TaskItem? Update(int id, string title, bool done);
bool Delete(int id);
and a class `InMemoryTaskStore : ITaskStore` that keeps its tasks in a private list.
| Method | Behaviour |
| constructor | no parameters. A new store holds the same three starting tasks as before (ids 1, 2, 3). |
| `GetAll()` | every task in id order, as a copy of the list |
| `Get(id)` | the task, or `null` when there is none |
| `Add(title)` | creates a task with the next id (highest + 1) and `Done` false, stores it, returns it |
| `Update(id, title, done)` | replaces the title and done state, returns the updated task, or `null` when there is none |
| `Delete(id)` | removes the task. `true` when it existed, `false` when not. |
The store does not validate titles. Deciding what a client may send is the endpoint's job.
Guard every method with a `lock`, because one store will serve all requests.
Then register it, before `builder.Build()`:
```csharp
builder.Services.AddSingleton<ITaskStore, InMemoryTaskStore>();
All endpoints must keep working exactly as they do now.

// "1,2,3" for a JSON array of tasks, so one row can check which tasks came back and in what order.
static string Ids(JsonElement json) => json.ValueKind == JsonValueKind.Array
? string.Join(",", json.EnumerateArray().Select(e => DojoWeb.Prop(e, "id")))
: "(not a JSON array)";
static JsonElement At(JsonElement json, int index) =>
json.ValueKind == JsonValueKind.Array && index < json.GetArrayLength() ? json[index] : default;
static async Task<string> IdsOf(HttpClient http, string url) => Ids(await DojoWeb.Json(await http.GetAsync(url)));
static bool HasError(JsonElement json) => !string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(DojoWeb.Prop(json, "error"));
static Task<HttpResponseMessage> Patch(HttpClient http, string url, object body) =>
http.PatchAsync(url, JsonContent.Create(body));
static string? Field(object? value, string name) =>
value is null ? null : DojoWeb.Prop(JsonSerializer.SerializeToElement(value, value.GetType()), name);

require.message: Registers the store with AddSingleton<ITaskStore, InMemoryTaskStore>()

hints: The class body is code you already have: `Get` is the `FirstOrDefault` from `GET /tasks/{id}`, `Add` is the id calculation from `POST`, `Update` is the `FindIndex` and `with` from `PUT`, `Delete` is the `RemoveAll`.

Give the class two private fields: `private readonly object _gate = new();` and `private readonly List<TaskItem> _tasks = new() { new(1, "Learn C#", true), ... };`. Wrap each method body in `lock (_gate) { ... }`.

For example: `public TaskItem? Get(int id) { lock (_gate) return _tasks.FirstOrDefault(t => t.Id == id); }` and `public bool Delete(int id) { lock (_gate) return _tasks.RemoveAll(t => t.Id == id) > 0; }`

steps.title: Inject the store
prompt: Now switch every `/tasks` endpoint over to the store, and delete the `tasks` list from the top of `Program.cs`.
Each handler asks for the store as a parameter:
```csharp
app.MapGet("/tasks/{id:int}", (int id, ITaskStore store) =>
var task = store.Get(id);
return task is null ? Results.NotFound() : Results.Ok(task);
- All six endpoints (`GET /tasks`, `GET /tasks/{id}`, `POST`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, `PATCH .../done`) take an `ITaskStore` parameter and do their storage work through it.
- No endpoint may use a list, or a store object, held in a variable of `Program.cs`. The container supplies the store.
- Validation, filtering and paging stay in the endpoints. They are about HTTP, not about storage.
- For `PATCH`, the store has no method that changes only `done`. Read the task with `Get`, then call `Update` with its current title.

Seen from outside, nothing changes: every request gets the same response as before. The tests check all of it again. They also send 20 `POST` requests at the same moment, which is what the `lock` in your store is for.

|| (f.FieldType.IsGenericType && f.FieldType.GetGenericTypeDefinition() == typeof(List<>) && f.FieldType.GetGenericArguments()[0].Name == "TaskItem"))

// "1,2,3" for a JSON array of tasks, so one row can check which tasks came back and in what order.
static string Ids(JsonElement json) => json.ValueKind == JsonValueKind.Array
? string.Join(",", json.EnumerateArray().Select(e => DojoWeb.Prop(e, "id")))
: "(not a JSON array)";
static JsonElement At(JsonElement json, int index) =>
json.ValueKind == JsonValueKind.Array && index < json.GetArrayLength() ? json[index] : default;
static async Task<string> IdsOf(HttpClient http, string url) => Ids(await DojoWeb.Json(await http.GetAsync(url)));
static bool HasError(JsonElement json) => !string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(DojoWeb.Prop(json, "error"));
static Task<HttpResponseMessage> Patch(HttpClient http, string url, object body) =>
http.PatchAsync(url, JsonContent.Create(body));
